entries.title: Inuktitut at a glance
body: Inuktitut is the language of the Inuit of the eastern Canadian Arctic, spoken by about 40,000 people. It is an official language of Nunavut and of the Northwest Territories, and is used in schools, government and media there.

Inuktitut is polysynthetic: a word is built from a root followed by a chain of endings, so one word can carry the meaning of a whole English sentence. ᑐᒃᑐᓯᐅᕆᐊᖃᖅᑐᖓ (tuktusiuriaqaqtunga) means “I have to go caribou hunting”.

entries.title: How syllabics work
body: Inuktitut in Nunavut is written in Canadian Aboriginal syllabics, first made for Cree in the 1840s and adapted for Inuktitut later in the century. Each consonant has one shape, and the way it is turned shows the vowel: pointing up for i, right for u, left for a.

A dot above a character makes the vowel long (ᐱ pi, ᐲ pii). A small raised character, written after a syllable, is a consonant with no vowel (ᑉ p). Inuktitut in Nunavik (Quebec) uses the same script; in Labrador and the western Arctic it is written in the Latin alphabet.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: Traditional numbers are based on fives and twenties. Today many speakers use English numbers above five.

entries.title: Place names
body: Many places in Nunavut carry their Inuktitut names, which describe the land: Iqaluit (ᐃᖃᓗᐃᑦ) means “many fish”, Nunavut (ᓄᓇᕗᑦ) “our land”, and Kangiqtugaapik (ᑲᖏᖅᑐᒑᐱᒃ, Clyde River) “nice little inlet”.
Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit (ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᔭᑐᖃᖏᑦ), traditional Inuit knowledge, is one of the guiding principles of the Nunavut government.

entries.title: One, two, and many
entries.body: Nouns mark number on the ending. The basic form is one thing as subject; a dual ending (often ‑uk / ‑ak) is for two; a plural ending (often ‑t / ‑it) is for three or more. An indefinite singular object often takes ‑mik.

entries.title: Possession: my, your, their
entries.body: Possessive endings attach to the noun. On ᐊᓈᓇ (anaana) “mother”: ᐊᓈᓇᒐ (anaanaga) “my mother”, ᐊᓈᓇᐃᑦ (anaanait) “your mother”, ᐊᓈᓇᖓ (anaananga) “his / her mother”. ᓄᓇᕗᑦ (nunavut) is “our land”.

entries.title: In, to, and from: ‑mi, ‑mut, ‑mit
entries.body: Place endings attach to the noun: ‑mi “in / at / on”, ‑mut “to”, ‑mit “from”. Matching question words are ᓇᓂ? (nani?) “where?”, ᓇᒧᑦ? (namut?) “to where?”, ᓇᑭᑦ? (nakit?) “from where?”.

entries.title: Present verbs: who does it
entries.body: A verb needs a root and a person ending. After a vowel the statement endings begin with j (‑junga “I”, ‑jutit “you”, ‑juq “he / she”). After a consonant they begin with t (‑tunga, ‑tutit, ‑tuq).

examples.e: I go / have just gone out

entries.title: Saying no: ‑nngit‑
entries.body: Put ‑nngit‑ in the verb before the person ending. It deletes a preceding consonant, and the statement ending then begins with t. On their own, ᐄ (ii) is “yes” and ᐋᒃᑲ (aakka) is “no”. The everyday reply ᖃᓄᐃᙱᑦᑐᖓ (qanuinngittunga) “I’m fine” is built with ‑nngit‑.

examples.e: I'm fine (lit. I am not somehow)
